children.value: Explain the logic behind and the process of hypothesis testing. In particular, explain what the p-value is and how it is used to draw conclusions.
Now that we understand the general idea of how statistical hypothesis testing works, let’s go back to each of the steps and delve slightly deeper, getting more details and learning some terminology.
Hypothesis Testing Step 1: Stating the Claims

children.label: Hypothesis Testing Step 1: Stating the Claims

children.value: In all three examples, our aim is to decide between two opposing points of view, claim 1 and claim 2. In hypothesis testing,

As we saw in the three examples, the null hypothesis suggests nothing special is going on; in other words, there is no change from the status quo, no difference from the traditional state of affairs, no relationship. In contrast, the alternative hypothesis disagrees with this, stating that something is going on, or there is a change from the status quo, or there is a difference from the traditional state of affairs. The alternative hypothesis,

children.html: HaH_aHa​

children.value: , usually represents what we want to check or what we suspect is really going on.
Let’s go back to our three examples and apply the new notation:

children.html: H0H_0H0​

children.value: : The proportion of smokers at Goodheart is 0.20.

children.html: HaH_aHa​

children.value: : The proportion of smokers at Goodheart is less than 0.20.
In example 2 (concentration of a chemical in a drug):

children.html: H0H_0H0​

children.value: : The mean concentration in the shipment is the required 245 ppm.

children.html: HaH_aHa​

children.value: : The mean concentration in the shipment is not the required 245 ppm.

children.html: H0H_0H0​

children.value: : Performance on the SAT is not related to gender (males and females score the same).

children.html: HaH_aHa​

children.value: : Performance on the SAT is related to gender—males score higher.
Check Your Understanding: Identifying Null and Alternative Hypotheses

children.label: Check Your Understanding: Identifying Null and Alternative Hypotheses

children.value: According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the proportion of U.S. adults age 25 or older who smoke is 0.22. A researcher suspects that the rate is lower among U.S. adults 25 or older who have a bachelor’s degree or higher education level.

model.question: What are the appropriate hypotheses for this study?

choices.text: H₀: the proportion of college-graduate smokers is 0.22; Hₐ: the proportion is less than 0.22
choices.feedback: Correct! H₀ says the rate among college graduates is the same as the overall rate (0.22); Hₐ says it is lower, as the researcher suspects.

choices.text: H₀: the proportion is less than 0.22; Hₐ: the proportion is 0.22
choices.feedback: This reverses the roles—the researcher's suspicion belongs in the alternative hypothesis, not the null.

choices.text: H₀: the proportion is 0.22; Hₐ: the proportion is not 0.22
choices.feedback: The alternative should be directional ("lower") because the researcher specifically suspects a lower rate.

model.hint: The null hypothesis says "nothing special is going on" among college graduates; the alternative captures the researcher's suspicion.

children.value: A study investigated whether there are differences between the mean IQ level of people who were reared by their biological parents and those who were reared by someone else.

model.question: What are the appropriate hypotheses for this study?

choices.text: H₀: the two groups have the same mean IQ; Hₐ: the two groups have different mean IQs
choices.feedback: Correct! H₀ says there is no difference between the two means; Hₐ says the means differ (in either direction), since no particular direction was suspected.

choices.text: H₀: the two groups have the same mean IQ; Hₐ: those reared by biological parents have a higher mean IQ
choices.feedback: The study did not suspect a particular direction, so the alternative should be two-sided.

choices.text: H₀: the two groups have different mean IQs; Hₐ: the two groups have the same mean IQ
choices.feedback: The null hypothesis is always the "no difference / nothing special" claim.

model.hint: No direction is suspected here—the study simply asks whether there is a difference.

children.value: Check Your Understanding: Hypotheses in Context

children.label: Check Your Understanding: Hypotheses in Context

children.value: Data were collected in order to determine whether there is a relationship between a person’s level of education and whether or not the person is a smoker.

model.question: What are the appropriate hypotheses for this study?

choices.text: H₀: there is no relationship between education level and smoking; Hₐ: there is a relationship
choices.feedback: Correct! H₀: there is no relationship between level of education and smoking; Hₐ: there is a relationship.

choices.text: H₀: there is a relationship between education level and smoking; Hₐ: there is no relationship
choices.feedback: This reverses the roles of the null and alternative hypotheses.

choices.text: H₀: more-educated people smoke less; Hₐ: more-educated people smoke more
choices.feedback: No direction was specified in the research question, and hypotheses about relationships between two categorical variables are stated in terms of relationship/no relationship.

model.hint: The null hypothesis is the "no relationship" claim.

Hypothesis Testing Step 3: Assessing the Evidence

children.label: Hypothesis Testing Step 3: Assessing the Evidence

children.value: As we saw, this is the step where we calculate how likely it is to get data like that observed when

children.html: H0H_0H0​

children.value: is true. In a sense, this is the heart of the process, since we draw our conclusions based on this probability. If this probability is very small (see example 2), then that means that it would be very surprising to get data like that observed if

children.html: H0H_0H0​

children.value: were true. The fact that we
observe such data is therefore evidence against

Obviously, the smaller the p-value, the more surprising it is to get data like ours when

children.value: Right now we will not go into specific details about p-value calculations, but just mention that since the p-value is the probability of getting

children.html: H0H_0H0​

children.value: is true, it would make sense that the calculation of the p-value will be based on the data summary, which, as we mentioned, is the test statistic. Indeed, this is the case. In practice, we will mostly use software to provide the p-value for us.

It should be noted that in the past, before statistical software was such an integral part of introductory statistics courses, it was common to use critical values (rather than p-values) in order to assess the evidence provided by the data. While this course focuses on p-values, the critical values approach leads to the same conclusions.
